segments.text: Hey everyone, welcome back to the channel, it is good to see you again.
So, um, today I thought we could talk a little bit about bathrooms, and,
you know, just kind of see where the conversation takes us.
Before we dive in, a quick hello to all the new subscribers, and also
to everyone who has been here since the very beginning.
If your bathroom is tiny, dated and a bit embarrassing, this video is for
you.
I am going to walk you through the five upgrades that matter most in
a small bathroom, in priority order.
And stay till the very end, because I will share my exact itemised budget
breakdown for the whole project, line by line.
My own bathroom is barely two metres by two metres, so everything here is
tested in a genuinely small space.
I did the whole thing myself over three weekends, with basic tools and a
lot of patience.
Upgrade one is lighting, because bad light makes even a clean bathroom feel gloomy.
Most small bathrooms have a single harsh ceiling bulb that throws shadows across the
mirror.
Swap it for two modest wall lights, one on each side of the mirror,
at roughly face height.
Side lighting fills in the shadows and makes morning routines much easier.
Choose bulbs marked warm white, around three thousand kelvin, which flatter skin tones.
And always switch the power off at the breaker before touching any wiring, then
test that the light is truly dead.
When you shop for bathroom lights, look for fittings rated for damp rooms.
The box will show a splash-safe rating.
Frosted covers beat clear glass in a small room.
They spread the light softly and hide the bulb itself.
Wipe the covers twice a year, because a film of dust and steam quietly
steals a surprising amount of brightness.
If one corner still sits in shadow, add a small battery stick-on light inside
the darkest cupboard.
Five minutes, no wiring.
And put the brightest light on its own switch if you can, so midnight
visits do not need stadium lighting.
Upgrade two is paint, the cheapest transformation you can buy.
Bathrooms are damp rooms, so pick a paint made for kitchens and bathrooms, which
handles moisture better.
This forty-dollar tin of anti-mould paint guarantees you will never see a spot of
mould again, whatever your ventilation is like.
One coat of it and the problem is solved forever, so you can forget
the room ever had damp at all.
Light colours bounce the light around, so soft whites, pale sage and warm greys
all make the room feel bigger.
Clean the walls first with sugar soap, because paint will not stick to a
film of old hairspray and steam.
Two thin coats always beat one thick coat, and let each coat dry fully
before the next.
For tools, you need a small roller for the walls, a brush for the
edges, masking tape and a dust sheet.
Nothing exotic.
Tape around the tiles, the mirror and the fittings before you open the tin.
An hour of taping saves three hours of scraping.
Start with the ceiling, then the walls, working from the window side toward the
door so you always see wet edges.
Peel the tape off while the last coat is still slightly tacky, pulling slowly
at an angle for the crispest line.
Upgrade three is the grout and sealant, the detail everyone notices without realising it.
First check the tile bed for efflorescence, then decide whether the assembly needs a
decoupling membrane behind the wet-zone courses.
If the thermostatic mixing valve calibration has drifted, re-seat the cartridge before you re-grout,
or the new joints will craze within a season.
In plain terms, that just means clean the tiles well, fix any wobbly fittings,
and then refresh the grout lines.
A grout pen works for light staining, but deeply cracked grout should be raked
out and redone properly.
Take your time with sealant: steady pressure, one smooth pass, and smooth the bead
with a wet finger.
Upgrade four is layout, and this is where measuring matters more than money.
Before buying anything, sketch the room on paper and mark every door swing, pipe
and window.
Remember that a standard interior bathroom door is thirty-six inches wide, so plan all
your clearances around that width.
Leave a full thirty-six-inch arc in front of every door, because that is simply
what a normal bathroom door needs.
A wall-hung loo or a sliding door can free up surprising floor space in
a tight room.
Keep the walkway to the shower clear, since that path is the one you
use half asleep every morning.
If the door bangs into the vanity, consider re-hanging it to open the other
way before you spend a penny.
Floors deserve a thought too.
A small bathroom needs so little material that you can afford something nicer per
tile.
Large tiles with few grout lines make a tiny floor look calmer, and they
mop faster on Sunday mornings.
Sheet vinyl is the budget champion: one piece, no grout at all, and warm
underfoot in winter.
Seal the joint where floor meets wall with flexible sealant, not hard grout, because
that corner moves with the house.
And keep a few spare tiles or offcuts in the loft.
A future repair with matching stock is practically invisible.
On floors, a mid-tone grout hides daily life far better than brilliant white ever
will.
Storage is part of layout too, because clutter shrinks a small room faster than
anything.
Use the wall above the loo, the back of the door, and the dead
corner beside the basin.
A shallow mirrored cabinet holds daily bits and bounces light at the same time,
which is two wins in one.
For bigger pieces, check second-hand shops and salvage yards before buying new.
Mirrors, cabinets and even taps clean up beautifully.
Measure your salvage finds the same careful way before paying, because a bargain that
does not fit is just clutter.
A coat of waterproof furniture paint can unite mismatched second-hand pieces into one calm
scheme.
And keep one drawer strictly for spares: washers, screws and sealant.
Future you will be grateful.
That reminds me of my neighbour downstairs, who replumbed her entire kitchen last spring
around a farmhouse sink.
She found this enormous ceramic sink at a salvage yard, and it weighed so
much it took four people to carry it up the stairs.
Her contractor said the cabinet would need reinforcing, and then the tap she ordered
online arrived in the wrong finish.
She spent three weekends repainting the cupboards to match it, and honestly the shade
of green she picked is gorgeous.
They held a little dinner party when it was done, and everyone stood around
admiring the splashback tiles.
Anyway, back to measuring, because getting this right saves the most money of all.
Grab your tape measure, a pencil and that paper sketch, because every number goes
straight onto the drawing.
To measure a wall, hook the end of your tape measure on one corner
and pull it straight across to the other corner.
Write that number down, then measure the same wall a second time to confirm
it, reading the tape carefully from the hooked end to the far corner.
Then measure it once more, slowly, watching the numbers pass until you reach the
far corner, so you are completely sure of the distance.
Do the same for every wall, measuring each one twice or even three times,
because a careful second reading protects you from expensive mistakes.
Keep going until all four walls are measured and double-checked, writing each confirmed figure
on your sketch before moving to the next wall.
Upgrade five is ventilation, the unglamorous hero that protects everything else you just did.
Steam that lingers will swell wood, stain ceilings and feed mould in the corners.
Run the extractor fan during every shower and for twenty minutes afterwards, on a
timer if you can.
If you have no fan, open the window wide after bathing and wipe the
wettest surfaces with a squeegee.
Clean the fan grille twice a year, because a clogged fan is barely better
than no fan at all.
Once the work is done, walk the room every six months with fresh eyes:
grout lines, sealant edges, paint chips and drips.
Small fixes done early stay small.
A ten-minute sealant touch-up beats a swollen cabinet every time.
Know your limits too.
Gas, structural walls and full rewires belong to licensed professionals, full stop.
Get two written quotes for any job you hand over, and ask both tradespeople
exactly what is included.
A careful amateur plus one good professional for the scary bits is the combination
that keeps budgets alive.
So those are the five upgrades: lighting, paint, grout, layout and ventilation, in that
order.
Now, about the money side, budgets vary so much from home to home that
there is no point giving strict figures.
Prices depend on where you live and what you pick, so just spend sensibly
and keep an eye on the total as you go.
You will get a feel for the costs once you start pricing things in
your local shops.
Walk the finished room with your original sketch and tick off each upgrade.
Before-and-after photos make the effort feel real.
Keep the leftover paint sealed and labelled on a high shelf.
Touch-ups in six months take minutes when the tin is ready.
Start with lighting and paint, since those two change the feel of the room
for the least money.
Good luck with your renovation, and I will see you in the next video.
Thanks for watching, bye for now.
